To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We developed and evaluated weighted estimators for improving disease incidence estimates in a primary care surveillance system.

(i) we observed an association between the number of consultations in GPs and the number of reported cases in a primary care surveillance system; (ii) this association was used to define several weighted incidence estimates; (iii) depending on hypotheses for weight computation, relative changes in incidence estimates between -40% to +55% were observed; and (iv) bias reduction was obtained using bias-reduced weights.
the use of external information on consultation rates in GPs improves incidence estimates in primary health care surveillance systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods to improve estimates of disease incidence from primary care surveillance systems.
the problem of bias reduction in primary care surveillance data and the development of new estimators for incidence.
improving estimates of the incidence of diseases, in primary care surveillance, using external information on consultations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method improves estimates of the incidence of influenza and varicella, while the effect on estimates of the incidence for diarrhea is less clear.
the Sentinelles network is a good tool for monitoring the incidence of influenza and varicella in France, and for diarrhea at the national level.
consultation-weighted incidence estimators can be used as a complement to traditional incidence estimates in order to improve the quality of primary care surveillance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Sentinelles system provides a reliable estimate of the incidence of influenza, varicella, and diarrhea in France.

the Sentinelles network is not as representative as we would have liked it to be, but we have a better understanding of the limitations of the data and we have developed tools to correct for some of these limitations.
the use of weights based on consultation volumes can improve estimates of the number of reported cases of influenza, diarrhea, and varicella in the Sentinelles network.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in such surveillance systems, incidence estimates are biased, but the bias is not constant over the study period.
the use of external data can improve the representativeness of primary care surveillance systems, and therefore, the reliability of incidence estimates.

the choice of a weighting scheme is crucial for surveillance systems based on the voluntary participation of health-care providers, especially when the population of interest is not representative of the general population.
